How to use these mocks

Each set contains eight prompts. Answer aloud before opening the model answer. Allow roughly five minutes per prompt including a follow-up, then review the gaps. These are original practice interviews based on the skills covered in this manual, not leaked employer questions or predictions of an exact interview. A short correct answer is better than a long list of features. The model answers show reasoning, not the only acceptable implementation.

Use a five-part score for each answer: correctness, requirement clarification, design reasoning, failure handling and evidence/testing. Give each dimension 0 for missing or wrong, 1 for partly explained, and 2 for a clear defensible explanation. This is a self-assessment rubric, not an employer pass threshold. A confident incorrect transaction or security claim matters more than forgetting a UI label.

Mock A — platform and SSA ownership

Questions A1–A8 below cover runtime, rule selection, case design, data, decisioning and delivery. After answering, sketch the rule or data context. If you can repeat a definition but cannot explain a failure, reread the associated lesson.

Mock B — integration and a GCC production role

Questions B1–B8 use events, services, concurrency and operations. Draw the time sequence around every commit and external call. Name the business effect you protect. Avoid saying “Kafka guarantees exactly once” or “we retry everything” without specifying the boundary.

Mock C — modern Pega and consulting delivery

Questions C1–C8 test Constellation, reusable design, customer communication, framework boundaries and safe AI use. Explain how you decide whether to configure, extend or build. A consultant needs to turn unclear requirements into a maintainable solution and communicate the consequences.

Incident drill 1: a payment appears twice

Evidence: two processing attempts share an upstream event ID, with a worker restart between them. Reasoning: replay after an uncertain acknowledgement is plausible, but the evidence does not yet prove where the duplicate financial effect occurred. Compare inbound receipts, database transaction results and downstream operation identities. Containment: restrict the affected replay or side-effect path with the incident owner, preserve evidence and avoid blindly clearing all queues. Correction: reconcile with the authoritative ledger and apply an approved business correction. Prevention: enforce durable operation identity at the appropriate side-effect boundary and test a crash after commit. A higher retry count does not fix duplicate effects.

Incident drill 2: account data stays stale after a payment

Evidence: the source is updated; one user's screen shows the old value; another request sees the new one. Reasoning: inspect source freshness, data-page scope and parameters, reload policy, editable copies and UI refresh. Do not assume the database is stale because the screen is. Correction: invalidate or refresh the correct data instance through the supported mechanism and ensure the view uses the intended source. Prevention: define freshness expectations and test update-then-read across users, threads and nodes. A node-scoped cache is not automatically cluster-wide shared state.

Incident drill 3: a rule works for one operator only

Evidence: same case type, different results under different users. Reasoning: compare application, access group, ruleset stack, version context, privileges, class, circumstances and effective dates. Use an authorized trace with the correct requestor. Correction: fix the intended application or authorization configuration, not a broad privilege grant. Prevention: test with representative roles. A selected rule failing authorization is not a request to search for a weaker accessible fallback.

Incident drill 4: backlog grows while workers look healthy

Evidence: nodes are running, failures are low, oldest-event age rises. Reasoning: compare arrival and completion rates; inspect connector latency, database waits, partitions, hot keys and expensive record types. “No failures” does not mean sufficient capacity. Correction: address the measured bottleneck and coordinate concurrency with downstream limits. Prevention: alert on age and net backlog growth, test a realistic distribution and document a drain-rate estimate. Scaling every worker can worsen a saturated database.

Incident drill 5: deployment succeeds but background work cannot find a rule

Evidence: the UI path works after deployment, but queued processing reports missing or unexpected rules. Reasoning: compare the background runtime application context and ruleset availability with the interactive requestor; inspect dependencies, rule versions and queued data compatibility. Correction: deploy the missing dependency or correct the intended runtime context through the approved process. Prevention: include a post-deploy background-work smoke test. Restarting nodes without knowing the context mismatch is not a root-cause fix.

Incident drill 6: a report is slow only after adding a column

Evidence: row count appears unchanged but elapsed time and database work rise. Reasoning: inspect generated SQL and whether the added property requires expensive extraction, a join or a per-row operation. Compare the plan and actual cardinality. Correction: adjust the report/query model or expose an approved property where justified; verify business output stays correct. Prevention: include representative data in report regression. A fast query returning incomplete rows is still a failed fix.

Incident drill 7: notifications succeed but the case shows failure

Evidence: the provider confirms an SMS was accepted, while the connector timed out. Reasoning: the external effect and local response are different events. Correction: correlate the provider operation ID, reconcile state and avoid generating a new action identity for a technical retry. Prevention: provider-supported idempotency, durable intent and explicit delivery states. A local rollback cannot unsend an SMS.

Incident drill 8: Constellation submits invalid data through an API

Evidence: the UI prevents a value, but a direct authorized API request accepts it. Reasoning: a browser validation or hidden field is not server-side business validation or authorization. Correction: enforce the requirement at the supported server-side action/data boundary and return a usable error. Prevention: test API and UI paths, including changed client payloads and cross-market access. Custom frontend code cannot be trusted to enforce the only control.

Incident drill 9: a queue retries the same malformed record forever

Evidence: repeated attempts fail on the same missing required field. Reasoning: this is a deterministic contract/data error, not a transient outage. Correction: quarantine with enough diagnostic context, identify the producer/mapping owner and correct data through a controlled process. Prevention: classify failures, bound retries and provide an audited replay after correction. Increasing retry frequency only spends more resources on the same known failure.

Incident drill 10: an AI-generated mapping passed a happy-path demo

Evidence: one example works, but decimals and missing fields fail later. Reasoning: the demo sampled too little of the contract. Correction: compare the draft with schema and mapping requirements, fix conversions, and test boundaries such as NULL, large values, dates and unexpected enums. Prevention: deterministic validation and human review before promotion. Model fluency and a clean demo are not correctness evidence.

The last recall test

Without looking, explain: case versus data; pattern versus directed inheritance; rule availability; data-page scope and freshness; declarative versus procedural logic; assignment versus stage; optimistic versus pessimistic locking; deferred save versus committed effect; connector versus service; QP versus Job Scheduler; partition ordering versus global ordering; retry versus replay; authentication versus authorization; RBAC versus ABAC; PAL versus Tracer versus database evidence; Constellation views versus traditional sections; unit versus integration testing; branch merge versus deployment; CDH eligibility versus arbitration; draft generation versus validated AI output.

Then take one real project and connect at least eight of those concepts. If you cannot, revisit the relevant chapter and solve its exercise. Reading every page is useful exposure; explaining mechanisms and completing the exercises is the evidence that you can use them.

Interview questions, fully answered

A1. What happens from a user action to execution of a Pega rule?

The request runs in a requestor/thread and application context with clipboard data. Pega identifies the appropriate rule using its class, rule type/name and applicable resolution context; assembled executable code and caches may serve execution. Rules can generate Java rather than simply being interpreted as XML on every call. The result may change clipboard state, invoke integration or persist work through the transaction owner. Follow-up: distinguish rule-selection problems from stale business data or an authorization failure.

A2. A specialized rule is not being selected. How do you investigate?

Confirm the exact rule call, primary/step page class, ruleset stack and allowed version, availability, circumstance values and effective date. Inspect a focused trace in the failing user's context and compare the candidate rules. Do not assume the numerically highest version always wins or clear every cache first. Follow-up: explain why an unavailable rule and a blocked rule do not mean the same thing.

A3. A settlement requires two independent approvals. Child cases or parallel assignments?

Clarify whether each approval has an independent owner, lifecycle, SLA and outcome that must be tracked separately. Parallel paths within the same case can handle coordinated approvals without separate case identity; child cases are appropriate for independently managed work. Define join/wait behavior, rejection, cancellation and data propagation. Follow-up: explain how one approver's update avoids overwriting another's work.

A4. Which data-page scope would you use for account details?

Start with who may share the data, the parameter keys, freshness and whether it is user-specific. Thread scope isolates a thread; requestor scope shares within that requestor; node scope is local to a node and must be suitable for shared data without user-specific leakage. Choose the smallest appropriate scope, then a deliberate reload policy. Follow-up: explain update-then-read behavior and why a copied editable page might remain stale.

A5. Decision table, data transform or activity?

Use a decision table for a transparent condition-to-result policy, a data transform for shaping or initializing data, and an activity for procedural orchestration where supported higher-level rules do not fit. Keep the business policy separate from side effects so it can be tested and governed. Follow-up: explain why moving every condition into one activity makes change review harder.

A6. Why does a report count too many cases?

Establish the intended grain and inspect joins to assignments or other one-to-many data. Compare a known case with multiple related records. Aggregate related data or change the query shape before joining; use distinct case identity only when it matches the intended metric. Follow-up: explain why COUNT(*) and COUNT(non-null child key) differ on an outer join.

A7. How do you secure a sensitive approval?

Authorize the action on the server using the appropriate role/privilege and contextual access rules, validate business state and inputs, and record who approved what. Protect related data, APIs, reports and attachments. Hiding the button is only a UI behavior. Follow-up: explain the difference between a user being authenticated and being allowed to approve this particular account.

A8. What proves a release is ready?

Evidence includes reviewed changes, resolved dependencies, relevant automated and manual tests, environment configuration, compatibility of existing work and a deployment/recovery plan. Guardrail score is one quality signal. After deployment, validate core business paths and background work with representative authorized roles. Follow-up: distinguish reverting rule code from reversing an already sent external instruction.

B1. A REST call times out after two seconds. What do you do?

Classify the operation and its possible side effect. A timeout means no timely response, not proof that nothing happened. Use a stable idempotency key or status lookup where the contract supports it; bound retries for transient failures and reconcile uncertain effects. Record correlation and sanitized context. Follow-up: explain why retrying a payment POST with a new key can be unsafe.

B2. Can Kafka guarantee that the business update happens exactly once?

Kafka has ordering and delivery/transaction mechanisms within defined boundaries, but a Pega database update or external service is another boundary. A worker can commit an effect and fail before acknowledging processing. Design durable business identity, atomic local updates where possible and recovery/reconciliation across systems. Follow-up: identify the point at which duplicate delivery becomes a duplicate business effect.

B3. How do you choose Queue Processor versus Job Scheduler?

Use a Queue Processor for independently queued work that needs asynchronous processing and configured retry/error handling. Use a Job Scheduler for work triggered on a schedule, often to find eligible items and enqueue bounded units. Define runtime context and execution scope for the installed version. Follow-up: avoid having every scheduled run process an unbounded entire table in one transaction.

B4. Two users and one worker update the same case. What is your design?

Identify which updates truly belong to the same work item and how conflicts should behave. Use the case's supported locking/concurrency strategy, keep updates brief and re-read/validate state before applying a business transition. A stale update must not silently overwrite newer data. Follow-up: do not hold a lock during a slow remote call unless the specific design justifies the availability cost.

B5. Processing is 222/s and input is 250/s. What does that mean?

The system is not keeping up under those averages; backlog grows around 28/s, about 100,800/hour. Confirm the windows and units, then inspect bottlenecks, error mix and key distribution. Increase sustainable capacity or reduce/admit load with business agreement. Follow-up: more threads help only if database, connector and ordering constraints allow it.

B6. A connector is slow. Which tools and evidence do you use?

Measure where end-to-end time is spent before choosing a fix. Use appropriate Pega performance data and alerts, focused tracing for the call path, connector timing and downstream correlation. Check connection/auth behavior, payload size, retries and service latency. Follow-up: separate queue wait from connector execution time so you do not blame the wrong component.

B7. Design a replay endpoint.

Require authorized scope and stable record IDs, validate eligibility, bound batch size and rate, and create an auditable operation identity. Reuse original business identity for retry; expose accepted, running, completed and failed states. Prevent deterministic failures from looping and reconcile uncertain side effects. Follow-up: explain how partial success is reported and how the caller safely retries the request.

B8. How do you prove that a migration lost no records?

Define the source population and time window, then reconcile stable identities, accepted/rejected/pending counts and relevant business totals. Account for late and duplicate events explicitly. Compare business state, not just HTTP 200 counts or number of messages read. Follow-up: decide how backfill is separated from live notifications and how mismatches are resolved.

C1. Explain Constellation to a team familiar with sections.

Constellation uses a prescribed, view-oriented UI architecture and DX API interaction model; traditional section/harness customization does not transfer directly. Model the case and data, use supported views and components, and extend through supported SDK mechanisms only for justified gaps. Follow-up: identify whether a UI issue is in view metadata, data/API response, authorization or a custom component.

C2. A client wants a completely custom screen. How do you respond?

Clarify the user task and the requirement the standard experience fails to meet. Demonstrate a supported configuration first, then evaluate an extension's accessibility, API compatibility, validation, tests and upgrade ownership. Explain the maintenance cost in user terms. Follow-up: do not promise that arbitrary DOM scripts are a supported Constellation customization strategy.

C3. How do you test a business decision?

Create deterministic inputs and expected outcomes around boundaries, priorities, missing values and combinations. Isolate external data where appropriate and verify the selected rule context. Add integration tests to prove the decision is invoked with the right inputs in the case. Follow-up: a unit test of a decision table cannot prove the connector maps currency correctly.

C4. How do you extend an industry framework?

Understand the provided lifecycle, data model and supported extension points for the installed version. Keep client-specific behavior in the application layer with clear reuse and minimal unnecessary forks. Test framework upgrades and dependent integrations. Follow-up: do not claim Smart Dispute deadlines or CLM policy values without the actual configured business/network requirements.

C5. Eligibility versus arbitration in CDH?

Eligibility determines whether an action is allowed for a customer under defined policy; other engagement-policy conditions and constraints further shape candidates. Arbitration ranks appropriate remaining candidates using the configured decisioning approach. A high score does not grant permission to bypass policy. Follow-up: distinguish a predicted response likelihood from proof that a treatment is suitable.

C6. Where would you use GenAI safely in a workflow?

Choose a bounded task such as drafting a summary or mapping proposal, define trusted inputs and authorized tools, validate outputs and retain human review where consequential. Treat retrieved text as data, not instructions that can override permissions. Measure task accuracy and failure cases. Follow-up: an agent must not be allowed to approve its own sensitive action merely because it generated a persuasive explanation.

C7. The product owner changes a requirement just before release. What do you do?

Clarify the business urgency and acceptance examples, estimate affected rules/data/tests and explain the release options with risks. Separate a small compatible change from one that changes in-flight work or contracts. Agree scope and validation with the responsible people, document the decision and verify the result. Follow-up: use a real example if asked about past behavior, not an invented success story.

C8. Why are you ready for broader responsibility?

Use your real evidence: ownership of a component, a defensible design decision, an incident you diagnosed, a quality improvement and collaboration across roles. Explain what you can own independently and when you involve an architect or specialist. Tie your APAC integration and operations experience to this job's actual scope. Follow-up: a salary target or certification by itself is not evidence of readiness.

Apply it

Worked exercise

Run all three mocks without reading answers first. Select the three weakest answers and rewrite them using a concrete requirement, a mechanism, a failure boundary and a validation step.

Read the worked solution

A completed exercise produces three explanations that another engineer can challenge and test. For example, improve 'I use QPs for performance' to: 'I queue this notification intent so the user does not wait for the provider. The case transaction records the intent; the worker uses a stable action key, bounded retries and a delivery state. I test a timeout after provider acceptance and verify that replay does not create a second business action.' Adapt the mechanism to the supported design you actually implement.

12. Deployment, CI/CD, Authentication, Locking & Production Internals / K. Real Production Issues: What You Will Actually Face / Authentication & Access

Authentication & Access — Source list items: SSO certificate expired: IdP certificate has validity period. All SSO logins fail when it expires. Fix: update cert in PEGA auth service or JVM truststore. | LDAP server unreachable: Network/DNS/firewall change or LDAP restart. All logins fail if LDAP is the only auth. Fix: check connectivity, DNS, firewall. | Operator locked out: Failed attempts exceed threshold → operator disabled. Admin re-enables. | Access group missing from app: After deployment, new AG not in application rule's list. Users on that AG get errors. | Privilege deleted during merge: Branch removed a privilege. Flow actions checking it fail silently (button disappears). | Session timeout too aggressive: Users lose unsaved work. Tune idle timeout DSS.

Expired signing/TLS certificates, LDAP connectivity, operator state, missing access configuration, privileges and timeouts are separate hypotheses; avoids claiming every expiry affects all users or every access failure is silent.

Provisioning, deprovisioning and security audit evidenceChapter 15 · Security: identity, authorization, attachments and secretsChapter 23 · From branch to production: releases, configuration, and recoveryChapter 16 · Debugging with evidence: Tracer, Clipboard, logs and UI tools
Corrected / qualifiedcsc-c095

12. Deployment, CI/CD, Authentication, Locking & Production Internals / K. Real Production Issues: What You Will Actually Face / Case Locking

Case Locking — Source list items: Stale locks from crashed sessions: Browser crash / network drop → lock remains until timeout. Other users blocked. | QP + user conflict: User has case open → QP tries to update → QP fails → items pile up. Fix: redesign so background updates happen at non-conflicting lifecycle points. | Bulk job during business hours: Batch job locks many cases sequentially. Users get blocked. Fix: schedule off-hours or use optimistic locking. | Admin force-unlock misuse: Someone releases lock while user is editing → user's save overwrites. Only release when certain holder is inactive.

Crashed holders, QP/user conflicts, bulk locking and force-unlock risks are taught; switching to optimistic locking is a design decision, not a universal safe batch fix.

Chapter 14 · Transactions, deferred saves and concurrent case updatesChapter 13 · Background processing: queue processors, schedulers and safe recovery
Corrected / qualifiedcsc-c096

12. Deployment, CI/CD, Authentication, Locking & Production Internals / K. Real Production Issues: What You Will Actually Face / Queue Processors

Queue Processors — Source list items: Stream node down: QP messages can't reach Kafka → fall back to DB queue → processing slows dramatically. | Poison message: One message causes repeated failures → retries forever → blocks partition. Fix: configure max retries + dead-letter handling. | Consumer lag: Incoming rate > processing rate → pending count grows. Fix: add nodes/partitions, optimize processing activity, fix external latency. | DB fallback buildup: Without stream nodes, pr_sys_queue table grows large → slows everything. Fix: ensure stream nodes are running.

Stream availability, poison records, lag and recovery are explained without assuming infinite retries, every poison item blocks a partition, or a particular DB table transparently replaces Kafka.

Chapter 13 · Background processing: queue processors, schedulers and safe recoveryChapter 12 · Kafka, data sets and data flows: ordering, recovery and real guaranteesChapter 18 · Resilient integration patterns and production runbooks
Corrected / qualifiedcsc-c097

12. Deployment, CI/CD, Authentication, Locking & Production Internals / K. Real Production Issues: What You Will Actually Face / Deployment

Deployment — Source list items: Missing rules in package: Rule was in branch but not merged before packaging. Feature broken in target env. | Data instance not included: Access group / work queue / DSS not in package. Feature deployed but config broken. | Ruleset version conflict: Target env has higher minor version already. Import skips rules. Fix: align versions or use skimming. | App setting overwritten: Package includes dev endpoint URL → overwrites production URL → all integrations break. | Cache stale after import: Old nodes still serve cached rules. Usually auto-invalidated but clustered envs may need rolling restart in rare cases.

Missing branch changes/configuration, visible version conflicts, settings and cache symptoms are diagnosed explicitly; a higher target minor version does not inherently mean import skips every rule and skimming/restarting is not a generic repair.

Chapter 23 · From branch to production: releases, configuration, and recoveryChapter 03 · Application stacks, rule resolution and controlled specialization
Corrected / qualifiedcsc-c098

12. Deployment, CI/CD, Authentication, Locking & Production Internals / K. Real Production Issues: What You Will Actually Face / Integration

Integration — Source list items: Certificate mismatch: Production API uses different SSL cert. PEGA JVM truststore doesn't have it → connection refused. | OAuth token not refreshing: Token cached, never refreshed. After expiry all calls fail. Fix: configure token refresh in auth profile. | Timeout too short under load: External API slower in prod. PEGA connector times out. Fix: tune timeout, add async/circuit breaker. | Firewall rule missing: New env, DevOps forgot to whitelist PEGA IP for external API. | Response schema changed: External team updated API. Response data transform maps wrong fields or fails.

TLS trust/hostname/network differences, OAuth grant/token lifetime, timeouts and schema change are covered; client credentials do not necessarily involve a refresh token, and longer timeouts alone do not establish resilience.

Chapter 11 · REST, SOAP and integration contracts that survive failuresChapter 15 · Security: identity, authorization, attachments and secretsChapter 18 · Resilient integration patterns and production runbooks
Corrected / qualifiedcsc-c099

12. Deployment, CI/CD, Authentication, Locking & Production Internals / K. Real Production Issues: What You Will Actually Face / Performance

Performance — Source list items: Unexposed property in report filter: Filter on BLOB-stored property → full table scan. Fix: expose property (creates real DB column + index). | Clipboard bloat: Data page loads 10K+ rows into memory per session → heap exhaustion → GC pauses. Fix: paginate, filter at source, use report definition. | Declare expression cascade: Declare triggers on frequently-changing property → re-evaluates entire chain every time. Fix: minimize triggers, review dependency graph. | N+1 connector calls: Flow loops over list calling API per item. 100 items = 100 HTTP calls. Fix: batch API or redesign.

BLOB/query-plan evidence, clipboard growth, declarative dependencies and N+1 calls are taught; source-side filters, pagination/batching and targeted indexes are validated separately.

Step-by-Step: Verify Data Flows Are In Progress — Source list items: Open Dev Studio. | Go to Configure → Decisioning → Decisions → Real-time Processing . | Open the Data Flows landing page. | Filter by Status . | Select/check In progress . | Verify every required data flow shows Status = In progress . | Check # Failures column for each data flow. | If failures are 0 and status is In progress, the data flow is healthy. | If status is not In progress, use the Manage action for that row and start/resume according to project SOP. | Refresh the page and confirm the status returns to In progress .

21. Real Production Ops Runbook: Data Flows, Queue Processors, and CMS Audit Checks / D. Step-by-Step: Check Queue Processors in Admin Studio

D. Step-by-Step: Check Queue Processors in Admin Studio — Source list items: Switch from Dev Studio to Admin Studio . | Go to Resources → Queue Processors . | Check high-level dashboard counts: total queue processors, broken items, ready-to-process items. | Open the Queue processors landing page. | Filter/sort by Broken descending. | For each queue processor with Broken > 0 , open the broken item details. | Read the exception/error message. Identify whether failure is due to data issue, lock issue, integration issue, rule error, or system issue. | Fix the root cause first. Do not blindly retry if the same error will happen again. | After fixing, use approved PEGA actions such as Retry , Resume , or project-specific reprocessing utility. | Refresh Queue Processor screen. | Confirm Broken = 0 . | Check Ready to process . It should become 0 or steadily decrease. | If Ready to process is stuck/increasing, check whether processor state is Running, stream node is healthy, external dependency is slow/down, or consumer lag exists.

Quick reference

The vocabulary, in plain language.

ABAC
Attribute-based access control: contextual policy based on subject, object or other attributes. It complements action permissions rather than being a UI filter.
Access group
Configuration linking a user's or process's application access and roles to its runtime context.
Activity
A procedural rule with ordered steps. Use it for justified orchestration rather than replacing every data or decision rule.
Assignment
A unit of work awaiting an operator or team action. Its routing, timing and completion contribute to case progress.
BLOB / Storage Stream
Serialized instance data stored in a database column. Frequently queried properties may need supported column optimization rather than repeated extraction.
Case
A business work item with lifecycle, state, accountability and outcomes. It is different from a reference data entity or transport message.
Circumstance
A rule specialization selected when the relevant context matches. It needs a deliberate fallback and test coverage.
Clipboard
Runtime pages and properties in a requestor/thread context. A clipboard value is not proof that the database has committed the same value.
Commit
The durable completion boundary for the local database transaction. It cannot atomically roll back unrelated remote effects.
Connector / Service
Outbound call from Pega / inbound request handled by Pega. Each needs an explicit contract and security context.
Constellation
Pega's view-oriented UI architecture with prescribed experiences and supported extension mechanisms; distinct from traditional section/harness customization.
CSSA / SSA
Certified Senior System Architect / Senior System Architect. Certification and job title do not imply production expertise in every Pega product.
Data Flow
A pipeline for reading, transforming and writing records using supported data-processing shapes and sources/sinks.
Data Page
A declared source and loading/cache behavior for application data. Scope, parameters, access mode and freshness determine correct use.
Data Set
A configured collection or source/destination of records used in supported data-processing operations; its capabilities depend on its type.
Data Transform
Rule for setting, mapping, copying or restructuring data. Keep business side effects and transaction ownership explicit.
Dead letter / Broken work
Work that cannot continue through its ordinary retry path. It needs diagnostic context, ownership and controlled correction/replay.
Declarative rule
A rule expressing a dependency or condition for platform-managed evaluation. Understand its configured trigger behavior rather than assuming it runs at every save.
DX API
Digital Experience API: supported interaction between a client experience and Pega application behavior/data; API generation and capabilities matter.
ECS
Enterprise Class Structure: organizing classes and reusable behavior across organizational and application layers.
Event time / Processing time
When the business event occurred / when the system processed it. Late arrival makes these different.
Idempotency
A repeated operation has the same intended effect as one operation under its contract. Responses can differ, and identity must remain stable across retries.
Inbox / Outbox
Application integration patterns for durable receipt/intent and reliable dispatch. They are design patterns, not a claim that every Pega application supplies them automatically.
Job Scheduler
A scheduled background trigger. Define execution scope, runtime context and bounded work for the installed release.
Kafka partition
An ordered log segment within a topic. Ordering within it does not create one global order across all partitions.
Locking
Coordinating competing updates. Pessimistic and optimistic approaches trade waiting against conflict detection and retry.
NBA / CDH
Next-Best-Action / Customer Decision Hub: decisioning concepts and product scope for selecting appropriate actions using policy and configured arbitration.
OIDC / SAML / OAuth
OIDC and SAML support identity/federation scenarios; OAuth is an authorization framework. A token alone does not define the business permissions for every object.
PAL
Performance Analyzer: measurements that help compare processing cost and investigate where work is spent. Interpret them with a defined test action.
PDC
Pega Predictive Diagnostic Cloud: operational diagnostic and performance signals. Use business reconciliation alongside technical health indicators.
QP
Queue Processor: background processing of queued items with supported concurrency and failure handling. End-to-end business safety still requires correct design.
RBAC
Role-based access control: permissions associated with roles. Combine it with appropriate object/context checks and server-side enforcement.
Replay
Controlled reprocessing of selected prior work. Different from endlessly retrying every failure; requires eligibility, identity and audit.
Report Definition
A rule describing a query/report. Join cardinality, exposed properties, filters and execution plans affect correctness and cost.
Requestor / Thread
An execution/session context / a subordinate processing context with its own relevant pages and state. Do not assume every user action shares all data.
Rule resolution
Selection of the appropriate rule in the applicable class, application and specialization context.
Ruleset
A container/versioning boundary for rules. Application stacks and dependencies determine the rules available at runtime.
SLA
Service-level agreement: expected timing and escalation behavior for the configured work scope; verify calendar and time-zone requirements.
Snapshot / Delta
An absolute state observation / a change to apply. Duplicate, stale-event and gap handling must match that distinction.
System Runtime Context
The deliberate application context used for relevant background processing; it must include required rules and dependencies.
Tracer
Execution-event inspection for a chosen context and event set. Use targeted traces; a trace is not a substitute for a load profile.
Transaction owner
The layer responsible for deciding whether related local changes commit or roll back. Nested reusable logic should not silently fracture that boundary.

Reference notes

This manual was authored from the supplied masterclass, SSA portal, CSC guide, exact lead-architect HTML guide and resume (with the earlier Word reference also consulted), with technical checking against primary documentation. The older guides are references for topic coverage; this manual corrects identified contradictions and does not copy their fictional first-person stories into your experience.

Sources are listed with each chapter. Some public documentation is historical, redirected or available through indexed excerpts; chapter notes preserve those limits. URLs may change after this edition. Core explanations, examples, questions and solutions remain embedded here.

Verification

All 30 chapters, 293 answered questions and 30 solved exercises were checked for structure and source references. The chapter 27 SQLite lab was executed with its expected results. The separate CSC/CMS SQL Server fixture is an instructional example and was not executed in SQL Server. All 34 inline SVG diagrams were rendered and visually inspected, with automated checks for text fit and arrow geometry. Offline reader behavior, including chapter focus and diagram enlargement, was checked with a DOM interaction harness. A Windows browser-connection failure prevented a rendered browser inspection; no visual browser test is claimed.

No live Pega environment was used to execute the Pega exercises. Their solutions are instructional designs; exact configuration must be checked in the target release. The book is comprehensive for the stated interview scope, while framework implementation expertise still requires hands-on work.

Keep your notes

Export stores your chapter progress and notes in a small JSON backup. Import replaces the current progress and notes with that backup. The handbook itself stays one self-contained HTML file.
